source.title: Mildly Overparameterized ReLU Networks Have a Favorable Loss Landscape
source.authors: Kedar Karhadkar; Michael Murray; Hanna Tseran; Guido Montúfar

record.file_problem: Full paper text supplied, including appendices; no apparent cutoff.
record.tranche_reason: Analyzes whether overparameterized ReLU networks have favorable loss landscapes and experimentally measures Jacobian rank and whether activation regions contain zero-loss minima. It does not directly test the benchmark classification-error claim or train networks to convergence in most experiments.
record.gate_note: Most results concern local landscape properties or the fraction of activation regions containing minima, not gradient training outcomes. The MNIST experiment does report gradient-descent outcomes and is included. Theoretical results are recorded as explicit text findings; cited prior work is excluded.
record.test_reason: The study measures loss-landscape geometry and the existence of interpolating solutions, rather than gradient descent's frequency of reaching spurious minima in V2. Its MNIST experiment measures cross-entropy convergence in shallow fully connected networks, rather than training classification error in the convolutional CIFAR networks named in V1. No own results test V3–V6.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is broadly accurate. The authors conclude that mild width overparameterization makes regions containing bad minima scarce, with their strongest results for shallow univariate networks. Qualify this by distinguishing counts of all potential activation patterns from counts of realizable regions; volume guarantees require additional data assumptions. These are landscape statements, not guarantees that gradient descent reaches global minima.
record.recipe_differences: The paper studies squared-error loss and activation-region/Jacobian properties of ReLU networks, with limited gradient-descent experiments on MNIST; the versions concern benchmark classification error and specified interventions or training recipes.
record.method_sensitivity: Results vary with input dimension, width, data-label construction, and (for one-dimensional inputs) data distribution; the text reports more interpolating regions for parabola data than for teacher-network or random labels.

fits_no_version.finding: The width needed for high probability of full Jacobian rank increases approximately linearly with sample count at fixed input dimension; larger input dimensions reduce the required width.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Width and input dimension govern the probability of a full-rank initialization Jacobian in shallow ReLU networks.

fits_no_version.finding: For univariate inputs, the empirical width threshold for most sampled regions to contain zero-loss solutions is close to n log n; parabola targets yield more interpolating regions than teacher-network or random targets.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The prevalence of interpolating activation regions depends on width and target construction.

fits_no_version.finding: The authors report that most sampled activation regions contain global minima in the higher-dimensional experiments.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Many randomly initialized activation regions contain interpolating solutions in the tested shallow ReLU regression settings.

fits_no_version.finding: Figure 9(b) measures the percentage of 100 random Gaussian initializations reaching cross-entropy loss at most 0.01 after 1000 epochs of gradient descent on MNIST; the percentages cannot be read from the supplied text.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Shallow fully connected ReLU networks can be evaluated for low-loss training success on MNIST as width and sample count vary.

fits_no_version.finding: Theorems bound unfavorable activation patterns under width conditions; stronger univariate results cover realizable regions, global-minimizer sets, and nonsmooth minima. Volume guarantees additionally require data-separation or anticoncentration assumptions.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Mild width overparameterization makes unfavorable activation regions scarce under specified geometric and distributional conditions.

record.problems: Most experiments measure Jacobian rank or whether sampled regions contain a minimum, not whether optimization reaches it. Figures supply the exact empirical percentages without tabulated values. The MNIST experiment reports cross-entropy loss, not classification error, and its plotted percentages are not stated in text. The paper itself identifies its strongest results as shallow one-dimensional cases and leaves strengthening deep-network and high-dimensional results to future work.
record.rows_left_out: No eligible result rows omitted. Figure 9(a)'s initialization-time Jacobian rank is not a training outcome and is not separately extracted because it does not bear on a listed version.

untested.parts: Training classification error of large convolutional networks on CIFAR-10/CIFAR-100, including corrupted labels, and comparisons with smaller or regularized models.
Gradient descent's spurious-minimum frequency as teacher and student widths grow together, and its reduction when the student receives one or two additional neurons.
Depth-dependent training degradation and comparisons involving identity shortcuts, special tanh initializations, or Fixup.
Effects of alternative initializations on learning speed, signal propagation, and trainable depth.
Loss and curvature trajectories relative to learning-rate stability thresholds, including recovery and divergence.
Training speed and learning-rate tolerance with versus without batch normalization, including Fixup comparisons.

record.verdict_notes: The supplied text contains figure captions but no readable heatmap values. No numerical success percentages or condition-specific verdicts can be inferred. Related findings do not establish absence or reversal of any listed version.

versions.untested_parts: No CIFAR experiments; no corrupted or random-label classification benchmark results. The MNIST experiment uses random Gaussian initialization and gradient descent and reports cross-entropy loss after 1000 epochs, but not training classification error.
The paper mentions Safran and Shamir as prior work but does not test teacher-student spurious-minimum rates as widths grow or compare student widths above teacher width.
No comparison of plain networks with and without identity shortcuts for training error.
Initialization procedures are used in experiments, but initialization effects on training speed or trainable depth are not compared.
No learning-rate-above-stability experiments or curvature tracking.
